facts.statement: Atlascopcosaurus was a small, herbivorous basal iguanodont dinosaur that lived in Australia during the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Atlascopcosaurus () is a genus of herbivorous basal iguanodont dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous Eumeralla Formation of Australia.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Atlascopcosaurus was discovered in 1984 at the Dinosaur Cove East site on the coast of Victoria, Australia.
facts.quote: The type specimen, NMV P166409, was found in 1984 at the Dinosaur Cove East site on the coast of Victoria, in layers of the Eumeralla Formation dating from the early Cretaceous, Aptian-Albian.

facts.statement: Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich named and described the species Atlascopcosaurus loadsi in 1989.
facts.quote: The type species, Atlascopcosaurus loadsi, was named and described by Tom Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich in 1989.

facts.statement: The genus name Atlascopcosaurus honors the Atlas Copco Company, which supplied equipment for the excavation where the dinosaur was found.
facts.quote: The generic name refers to the Atlas Copco Company which had provided equipment for the dig that discovered this dinosaur in 1984.

facts.statement: The specific name loadsi honors William Loads, the state manager for Atlas Copco who assisted during the excavation.
facts.quote: The specific name, loadsi, honours William Loads, the state manager for Atlas Copco at the time, who assisted during the dig.

facts.statement: The holotype of Atlascopcosaurus consists of a partial upper jaw with teeth, along with referred specimens of teeth, another maxilla, and dentaries.
facts.quote: The holotype consists of a piece of the upper jaw, a partial maxilla with teeth, and referred specimens include teeth, another maxilla, and dentaries.

facts.statement: Based on closely related species, Atlascopcosaurus is inferred to have been a small, bipedal herbivore, though most of its skeleton is unknown.
facts.quote: Although the rest of the skeleton is unknown it can be inferred from closely related species that the genus represents a small bipedal herbivore.

facts.statement: Boyd (2015) considered the genus valid and placed it at the base of Iguanodontia in a clade with Anabisetia, Gasparinisaura, and Qantassaurus.
facts.quote: However, Boyd (2015) considered the genus valid and recovered it at the base of Iguanodontia in a clade with Anabisetia, Gasparinisaura, and Qantassaurus.

facts.statement: The time range for Atlascopcosaurus is estimated from the Barremian to the Albian stages, between 125.77 and 110.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Albian (125.77 to 110.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: Atlascopcosaurus was originally assigned to the family Hypsilophodontidae in 1988, but this group is now considered unnatural and polyphyletic, with the species viewed as a basal member of Euornithopoda.
facts.quote: Atlascopcosaurus fue en 1988 asignado a la familia Hypsilophodontidae. Estos son hoy vistos como un grupo no natural, polifilético y ahora simplemente considerado como un miembro basal de los Euornithopoda.

facts.statement: Since the rest of the skeleton is unknown, it is inferred from closely related species that Atlascopcosaurus represents a small bipedal herbivore.
facts.quote: Como el resto del esqueleto permanece sin descubrir que sólo pueden ser inferidas a partir de especies estrechamente relacionadas que el género, representa un pequeño herbívoro bípedo.

rejected.statement: Extrapolations suggest Atlascopcosaurus loadsi was approximately 2 to 3 meters long and weighed about 125 kilograms.
rejected.quote: By extrapolation it has been estimated that Atlascopcosaurus loadsi was about two to three metres (6.5–10 ft) long and weighed approximately 125 kg.

rejected.statement: Agnolin et al. (2010) treated Atlascopcosaurus as a nomen dubium because its teeth are not species-specific and the maxilla fragment is uninformative.
rejected.quote: Because the teeth are not species-specific and the maxilla fragment is little informative, Agnolin et al. (2010) treated it as a nomen dubium, even though they noted similarities with the elasmarians Anabisetia and Gasparinisaura from Patagonia.
